# Laws Are Only Approximations

But as the sciences have developed farther, the notion has gained ground that most, perhaps all, of our laws are only approximations.[^1] The laws themselves, moreover, have grown so numerous that there is no counting them; and so many rival formulations are proposed in all the branches of science that investigators have become accustomed to the notion that no theory is absolutely a transcript of reality, but that any one of them may from some point of view be useful.[^2] Their great use is to summarize old facts and to lead to new ones.[^3] They are only a man-made language, a conceptual shorthand, as someone calls them, in which we write our reports of nature; and languages, as is well known, tolerate much choice of expression and many dialects.[^4]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "But as the sciences have developed farther, the notion has gained ground that most, perhaps all, of our laws are only approximations."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "The laws themselves, moreover, have grown so numerous that there is no counting them; and so many rival formulations are proposed in all the branches of science that investigators have become accustomed to the notion that no theory is absolutely a transcript of reality, but that any one of them may from some point of view be useful."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Their great use is to summarize old facts and to lead to new ones."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "They are only a man-made language, a conceptual shorthand, as someone calls them, in which we write our reports of nature; and languages, as is well known, tolerate much choice of expression and many dialects."
